Facu couldn't hold a front lever for a single second in his first month with me.

Some weeks after that he sent me footage of it collapsing worse than the week before, on a week where he'd trained clean. I told him that wasn't a setback. His standard had gone up, so failure looked heavier now.

By month 5 he had a 90 degree handstand pushup. By month 12: weighted muscle-ups, and weighted handstand pushups with 70kg on the dip belt and 15kg on the pull.

None of that came from a program he followed alone. It came from filming every set, sending the ugly ones too, and letting someone else tell him what the footage actually meant instead of guessing by himself.

The pattern repeats with almost every client who actually improves: the ones who get better are the ones whose bad reps are on camera, not just the good ones.

If your training log only has your good days in it, you're not tracking progress. You're curating a highlight reel.

What's the last rep you filmed that you didn't want anyone to see?

i used to think discipline was one thing. it's four, and they don't run on the same fuel.
swipe.

"i trained alone in a garage because i found peace for the first time in my life."

I wrote that to myself years ago, typos and all, and I've never cleaned it up because the typos are part of what was true that night.

Growing up I got talked over a lot. Family, school, the people around me at the time, always some version of not serious enough, not worth listening to yet. I didn't fight it. I just went quiet and took it somewhere else.

That somewhere else was a garage, alone, with the door closed and music on. Nobody walked through it. Nobody had an opinion about my set. For the first time I wasn't performing for anyone's approval, I was just training.

I still think that's the actual origin of the discipline people ask me about now. Not motivation. Not a morning routine. A closed door and one hour where nobody's judgment could reach me.

If you're waiting for the version of your life where everyone finally takes you seriously before you start taking yourself seriously, stop waiting. Close a door. Start there.

Everyone says face your fears.

I think that advice is almost useless on its own.

What actually changed how I make decisions was doing the math on fear instead of just feeling it. Somewhere around 99% of the things I've been afraid of in the last ten years never happened. Not "worked out fine." Never happened at all. The client I was sure would cancel didn't. The move that was going to ruin the business didn't. The conversation I avoided for three weeks lasted four minutes and changed nothing.

The 1% that did happen was survivable every time. Painful, expensive sometimes, but survivable.

So the fear itself was never the accurate part. It was just loud. The accurate part was the ratio, and almost no one actually checks it.

Next time you're stuck on a decision because of what might go wrong, write down the specific thing you're afraid of, then find three times in your life you were afraid of something similar. Check what actually happened those three times.

Most of you are about to find out you've been negotiating with a threat that's already lost 99 times in a row.

A client of mine, works long hours in an office job in the UK, came to me wanting a training plan.

Eight months in, the number that actually moved wasn't his lifts. It was his drinking, down by roughly three quarters, tracked every single week on our calls.

I never gave him a rule about alcohol. What I gave him was a call every week where he had to say the real number out loud to another person, not just log it somewhere private and round it up in his head.

That's the part of coaching nobody puts in the sales page. It's not the workout split. It's not the meal plan. It's a standing appointment where you can't quietly let the bad week slide, because someone's going to ask.

If you've tried to fix a habit alone and it kept slipping, the plan probably wasn't the problem. The privacy was.

the 8 things i actually check when a client stalls. it's rarely effort.
swipe through.

There was a stretch a few years back where my girlfriend was covering the gas for our car because I didn't have it.

I was building the coaching business from nothing at the time, and looking back neither of us had much to spare. She didn't complain about it once. She just kept telling me to compare myself to where I was heading, not where I was standing, and to put one action a day toward that instead of waiting to feel ready.

That period cost us real things. Time with friends, money, a normal early twenties. I don't regret any of it, because I found out much later that that was actually how I enjoy living.

Here's the line I still say to myself, exactly how I said it to myself back then: "every time that I'm out of my comfort zone, the results are crazy and insanely much better that when I'm inside of my comfort zone because that's the beauty of being out of the comfort zone is that's where I realize my truly potential."

It reads like a run-on because I wrote it like one, in the moment, not for anyone else to read.

Two years after that, it felt like ten. That's usually the actual exchange rate on the sacrifice nobody warns you about.

I coach men 1:1, training and accountability both, for $3,000 to $5,000 depending on the program length.

That's not a starting price with a catch. It's what this actually costs to do properly: weekly calls all year, video review on every set you send and someone checking the parts of your life that wreck your training too. Sleep. Food. Stress. All of it.

I'm not going to apologize for the number or dress it up as an investment in your future self. It's a coaching program. You pay for it and show up every week and I make sure the plan changes the moment your life does because it always does.

If you're already training and still stuck the gap usually isn't information. You have access to more workouts than any generation before you. The gap is nobody's checking your work so you check it yourself generously and let yourself off the hook.

If that's where you're at, my DMs are open. Tell me what you've actually tried and I'll tell you straight if this is a fit.

A guy messaged me a few months into working together to say he had to pause. Army debt, a custody lawyer, no spare money for coaching that month.

Old me would've heard that as a lost client. What I actually did was offer him a one-off $50 plan instead of losing the relationship completely. No upsell. No "let's hop on a call to see what we can work out."

He came back full price five months later once things settled.

The lesson wasn't about being nice. It's that almost none of the "no"s I get in sales calls are actually no. They're "not right now, and I'm watching how you handle me saying that."

Every coach I know treats a pause as the deal dying. Across hundreds of sales calls, the ones that actually closed later were the ones I didn't chase, where I just made the door easy to walk back through.

If someone tells you not now, the worst thing you can do is disappear or discount. The second worst thing is push. The best thing is make staying in touch effortless and let time do the rest.
people think rest days are the cheat day of discipline. they're not. they're the test.

Early on I compared my prices to coaches charging way more than me and felt behind, like I hadn't earned the right to charge what they charged yet.

I had that backwards.

A client of mine, years into paying for coaching, once insisted on paying me more than my own price, because he said he valued the service more than what I was charging for it. That same client also told me flat out to analyze what I'm actually doing every day, because that's what determines the man I become, not the plan I say I'm following.

Cheap pricing doesn't attract people who value what you do. It attracts people who are shopping, and shoppers leave the second someone cheaper shows up.

The "mentalidad de pobre" I had wasn't about how much money was in my account. It was measuring my worth against someone else's number instead of building one I could actually defend.

If you're underpricing what you do to feel safe, you're not being humble. You're avoiding the conversation where you'd have to explain why you're worth more, and that conversation is the whole job.

sprinting and swimming won't build your muscle. they show it.

2 sessions a week will lean you out.

but with no muscle under it you just get smaller, that's why this only works on top of calisthenics.

the week looks like this:

1. calisthenics 3 days a week
this is where the muscle comes from. pull-ups, dips, push-ups, rows and squats, a little harder every week. one more rep, a harder progression or weight on a belt. sprints and swimming don't load your muscles enough to grow them

2. one sprint day
short and all out. 6 to 8 sprints of 10-15 seconds, walk back and rest until you feel fresh again. when the last ones get slower than the first ones you're done for the day

3. one swim day
hard efforts of 30-60 seconds, recover and repeat for about 20 minutes. the water pushes back on every stroke so your back, shoulders and core work the whole time and your joints don't take a beating. in open water never go alone

4. drop the long slow runs
an hour of running a few times a week stacked on training, work and short sleep is a lot of stress to recover from, and weeks of high cortisol can drag your testosterone down. short hard sessions give you the conditioning without eating your recovery

my free guide on testosterone is in the first comment.

most women think they're too weak for calisthenics.
what holds most of them back is coordination.

her goal was better posture, a stronger upper body and workouts she could do at home without a gym. one week in she was sore everywhere and still got up early on a sunday to finish the third workout instead of pushing it to monday.

her form broke down in the same four spots, and every fix was a cue. zero extra reps.

1. hanging scapula pulls
she was lifting from her hips. look up about 45° as you retract and split your body in two, chest up does the work and chest down stays quiet. no crunching the abs, no swinging the legs

2. squats
eyes about 45° down. look straight ahead and your neck takes the load

3. push-ups with the elbows flaring out
we dropped the full rep and kept only the negative, 4-5 seconds down and every negative counts as one rep

4. band rows
get tension on the band before you pull. full range isn't the goal in week one

quality over long sets. once the brain finds the position the strength shows up fast.

"i'll start properly in january"

i hear it every year around now, usually from someone who has already decided the next eight weeks don't count

january won't be short on motivation. you'll have plenty of it. the catch is you'll be starting from the worst version of you, after two months of client dinners, flights and "it's the holidays"

the people who have a good january are the ones who didn't write off november and december. they didn't train perfectly either. they kept two or three things alive. a couple of sessions a week, protein at breakfast, a walk most days

that's enough. it's boring, and you start the year from where you are now

restarting is always harder than starting. keep something small going

the strongest guys i coach don't live in the gym

most of them have a job that eats ten hours a day. they can't give the gym two more, so they train 45 minutes, three times a week, wherever they are. a park, the beach, the living room

this is the kind of session i'd start most of them on

10 min warm up
walk or easy jog, then shoulders, hips and wrists

25 min main block
pull-ups, dips and push-ups. fewer reps, better reps, and once that's easy you add load. a backpack, a weighted vest or a kettlebell does the job

10 min legs and core
kettlebell swings or goblet squats if you have one, lunges and hollow holds if you don't

that's it. you get your bodyweight, a couple of kettlebells and some fresh air, and you walk out with the rest of your day still yours

training outside became the flex for me. you look like you train and the gym stopped being your whole life

client dinner season is starting, so these are the questions i get every year

"do i skip the dinner?"
no. it's part of the job, and one night out was never the problem. the other six nights are where it gets decided

"what do i order?"
a protein and something green first, then eat whatever else you want. you'll eat less of the rest without trying

"and the drinks?"
pick a number before you sit down. two is a plan. "we'll see" is five

"should i train the next morning?"
if you slept, yes. if you didn't, go for a walk and train the day after. a bad session on four hours of sleep doesn't make up for anything

"what if there are three in one week?"
damage control. eat well at breakfast and lunch, keep the water up and don't try to compensate by starving the next day

december doesn't undo a year. the "i'll sort it out in january" that comes with it does

three things i get clients to try before touching their training

1. an eye mask
the room is never as dark as you think. a phone charging, the street light, the standby on the tv. one of my clients now takes his everywhere, airport included

2. mouth tape

i've been using them for a while now and i like them even more than the tape. they open the nose without the strips falling off at 3am

more reps is the reason a lot of men are tired and still soft

the belief goes like this. if 10 push-ups didn't change anything, do 30. if 30 didn't work, do 50 and add a sixth day

what actually happens is you get very good at being tired. the sessions get longer, your sleep gets worse and the body in the mirror looks the same

what i do with clients instead
keep the reps you can do clean and stop there. one of my clients put it better than me, "if you're struggling, only do two or three good ones"
once the clean reps get easy, add load. weighted dips, a vest on the pull-ups, a kettlebell on the squats
rest between sets like you mean it
three of those sessions a week beats six sessions of volume

the guys who switch to this usually train less and look more trained a few months later

people think coaching is getting a workout plan. most of my job happens on a call like this one

this is what a check-in with me looks like

during the week you send me videos of your sessions. i watch them before we talk

the first thing i ask is how you felt, how you slept and what got in the way. the workout comes after

then we go through the videos. i start with what's better than last time, then what i'd change and why, so you understand it instead of copying a cue

if the week was bad we don't pretend it wasn't. we look at what broke it, a trip, a deadline, a kid who didn't sleep, and adjust the plan to the week you actually have

we finish with three things for next week. only three. and i'll be messaging you before the next call to see how they're going

the plan is the easy part. the rest is having someone watching
